articles.title: Transit officials investigate 'unsafe' incident after 2 horses boarded public bus
articles.summary: Transit officials in Detroit said they are looking into a recent incident in which two horses were captured on video briefly boarding a public bus. The Detroit Department of Transportation (DDOT) said in a statement Tuesday that it is "aware of a recent incident where two horses were allowed to walk through a bus as it was pulled over at a bus stop." Ellessia Drew via Storyful - PHOTO: A still from video showing two horses boarding a public bus in Detroit on Nov. 7, 2026. Transit officials said they are looking into the recent incident. Video of the incident shows two people leading two saddled horses onto the bus while it was pulled over at the stop, then exiting from the rear doors several seconds later. "We are taking appropriate steps to address this incident as it is not consistent with DDOT policy and potentially creates an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for our passengers," DDOT said. The incident occurred Saturday along 7 Mile East near Strasburg Street. Ellessia Drew was driving down 7 Mile when she stopped to film the incident. "I was thinking, like, 'Oh my God, like what about the people on the bus? What if the horse used the bathroom on the bus? Like, what's going on?'" Drew told ABC Detroit affiliate WXYZ . Ellessia Drew via Storyful - PHOTO: A still from video showing two horses getting off a public bus in Detroit on Nov. 7, 2026. Transit officials said they are looking into the recent incident. The animals' owner, Jordan Williams, with the group Urban City Cowboys, told WXYZ that he has brought horses on Detroit buses before. "It's not my first rodeo," he told the station. He said he had been at an event giving children horseback rides on Saturday. When he saw the bus pull up, he said he asked the driver if he could take his "service animal" on board for a video, with the goal of highlighting Black cowboys in Detroit. "The point is just to bring light to the city that there are cowboys that look like us," Williams told WXZY. Zoo Atlanta's giant pandas Ping Ping, Fu Shuang make public debut According to Williams, there were two or three passengers on the bus at the time and nobody got hurt. "I hope DDOT looks at it as a joke like everyone else, and hopefully maybe come out to a rodeo," Williams told WXYZ. DDOT noted that only service animals are allowed on buses and "must be under control by the person with disabilities at all times, must not occupy a seat, and must either sit on the floor, or on the person's lap." articles.title: Top White House lawyer warns Dems that threats of oversight could be criminally probed
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the Trump administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress -- may amount to “blatant criminality.” White House counsel Will Scharf issued the warning in a letter dated Monday to Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee. Garcia most likely would chair the powerful panel in the new Democratic-controlled Congress that is seated in January. Garcia warned Trump officials to “lawyer up” as his party was on the way to stunning victories in last week's midterm election. In response, Scharf wrote that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality." The letter’s existence was first reported by Punchbowl News. Garcia said in response to the letter that “it appears Donald Trump has something to hide” and stressed that Congress’ investigative powers do not need the “permission of the White House.” “Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” Garcia said. “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse.” Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. The Republican president and his White House have long denied any wrongdoing. Garcia also wants to look at the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations . Other targets include Trump’s White House ballroom and other construction projects, as well as the Trump family’s role in mineral deals and Trump’s crypto dealings with special envoy Steve Witkoff. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a CNN interview that aired Sunday that “there could be” a crime to investigate if rhetoric from Democrats turned threatening. He appeared to strike a more conciliatory tone during an appearance in Missouri this week, saying “Congress has oversight authority. It always has, it always will. The Department of Justice, the federal government, works with Congress to address questions they have — whether it’s through subpoenas or letters — so we’re not going to stop working with Congress.” “Nothing I’ve said this weekend, or in the past, should suggest otherwise,” he added. Some lawmakers cautioned Democrats as well as the White House against overreaching. Outgoing Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, said he hopes Democrats don't squander their new powers on “stupid things.” “I hope they have real hearings about real things, not another Russiagate,” he said, referring to a previous congressional inquiry into ties between Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and Russia. Trump repeatedly denounced that investigation as a “hoax.” “I think there is some real corruption there around the fringes,” Massie said about Trump and some of those around the president. Massie lost his primary election to a Trump-backed GOP challenger. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., who is expected to be the next House Ethics Committee chairman, said he would not back down from any investigations because of warnings from the White House. “If they're trying to intimidate, at least for me, it’s not going to get me,” said DeSaulnier, who was a Republican before he switched to the Democratic Party in 2000. “I don’t work for a mafia, a mob organization.” ___ Associated Press writer Eric Tucker and AP video journalist Nathan Ellgren contributed to this report. articles.title: Jim Jordan looks to move Republicans beyond midterm rout
articles.summary: House Republicans on Tuesday tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their diminished conference in the next Congress, betting that a conservative spitfire — and onetime leadership nemesis — can restore the fight to a party battered by the midterms and scrambling for a path back to power. In brief comments right out of the gate, Jordan set the tenor of the coming clash, vowing to fight the ascendant Democrats on the size and scope of federal power — an issue that’s taken on fresh significance with the arrival of a new crop of democratic socialist members. “When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom,” Jordan told reporters in the Capitol shortly after his victory at a press conference where new leaders declined to take questions. “And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day." He has a steep climb ahead. Jordan’s task is not only to bring together the warring factions of a restive party demoralized by their election rout and sniping over who’s to blame but also to craft a message that will resonate with alienated voters ahead of the 2028 elections — all while defending President Trump from the myriad investigations the Democrats are promising into the president’s family, allies and administration. It was the size of the election losses, some Republicans said, that tipped the scales toward Jordan over Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the outgoing majority leader whose many years in the leadership ranks became a liability, rather than an asset, after the midterm landslide. “He represents change,” said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.). “He also has a very detailed plan on how we get out of the minority. He has excellent communication skills. He's viewed as a fighter, which he is, and I think the conference was ready for a different direction.” “If the election would have been closer last week,” he added, “I think the results could have been different today.” For Jordan, the ascension represents an extraordinary arc for a right-wing renegade who built a brand in the Capitol for taking on party leaders, not joining their ranks. The Ohio Republican is a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, a bloc of iconoclastic conservatives who have routinely butted heads with GOP leadership over government spending and, at times, blocked Republican legislation in an effort to yank the party further to the right. He is also chair of the House Judiciary Committee, a role he’s used to launch investigations into Democrats and other Trump political opponents. “Jim Jordan is a fighter. I think he doesn't mind saying the hard things, but he's level-headed, and he's going to be able to work with a lot of different personalities to stay focused on the mission and get the job done,” Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-S.C.) said. If Tuesday’s leadership elections were a referendum on the midterm results, however, they also didn’t supply the “clean slate” some GOP lawmakers were hoping for. Rep. Tom Emmer (Minn.), the Republican whip, fended off a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) to keep his post. And Rep. Lisa McClain (Mich.), the GOP conference chair, will also remain in place after beating back challenges from Republican Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.). “This Republican leadership team will expose the Democrats’ lies and show the American people their true colors as the radical communists that they are,” Emmer said after his win. Trump stayed out of the leadership races — an unusual move for a president who has exerted his influence in past contests. Many Republicans are blaming Trump’s policies — particularly the Iran war, global tariffs and a deportation surge — for dragging down GOP candidates in the midterms. Some even suggested they chose Jordan because he expressed a willingness to break from the president on certain issues. Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) said he asked Jordan what the Republican conference was going to do “now that we have to deal with a president who we're not sure … how he's going to go forward.” “I thought he gave a very good answer, which was instead of waiting to see what the president’s going to say, we lead. We lead with a message based on what we want to say, and that's what I've always tried to do myself. I mean, each individual has to know their individual district as well as possible,” McCormick said. “We’re independent thinkers, right? … I want to not worry about what the president says. I want to have my own opinion, and … what's funny is the president usually comes around to what I believe anyway. And if he doesn't, that's OK because we're not a cult. If everybody in the church agrees with everything the minister says, you're in a cult. We are not a cult. It's very high time to realize that. And it goes back to the Reagan rule, right? It's OK if you disagree with me on a certain percentage. We can still be on the same team,” he added. The leadership transition, from Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to Jordan, could not offer a more stark contrast in styles and personas. Johnson is a constitutional lawyer, prim and bespectacled, who often quotes Bible verses and borrowed church terminology in pledging to be a “servant leader.” Jordan is a former champion wrestler, still fit and muscular, who’s known for eschewing a blazer around the Capitol and jousting routinely with Democrats from his perch atop the Judiciary Committee. The House Freedom Caucus repeatedly tried to tap Jordan to run against former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), which he resisted. But after McCarthy was ousted, it spurred a contentious 2023 battle for the Speakership between Scalise and Jordan. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination for Speaker then, defeating Jordan in a secret-ballot vote. But, he later withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support to secure the gavel. Jordan was later chosen as the nominee for Speaker, but he repeatedly fell short of the votes needed to clinch the post. “It's almost like this is the right time for him,” Rep. Tom Cole (Okla.), a member of the House Republican Steering Committee and the top Republican on the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters after the vote. “I think we need, you know, a combat guy, so to speak. But he's as good at political combat as anybody I've ever seen. So I think he'll do an excellent job for us.” Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-N.Y.) also said she sees Jordan as a unifier despite his staunch conservatism. “Jim Jordan is somebody who's a fighter, somebody who's thoughtful when he speaks,” she said. “He's eloquent. He doesn't miss a beat. He's out there talking about the issues, talking about what people are thinking. I think he'll do a good job. Look, I'm one of the more centrist members. … He brings everybody together.” “I think the reason I had supported him for Speaker two years ago, I thought he was the one who could bring everybody together because he had relationships with more moderate members, with the Freedom Caucus folks, and everybody in between,” she added. “So I think you know he handles himself in a way that he can get the job done.” Congressional Democrats were quick to criticize the pick as another instance of the GOP conference committing itself to a far-right pick after an election that they view as a resounding rejection of Trump. “Stephen Miller and Jim Jordan,” Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) wrote on social media, noting the promotion of Trump’s White House adviser to chief of staff. “Republicans learned absolutely nothing from what happened a week ago, and are responding by elevating their most extreme voices to positions of power.” But GOP members defended the choice. “I think you look at our conference, we're a significantly more conservative conference than what we were coming into this,” Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.) said, referencing the number of moderate members who lost their reelection bids. “And I think if you look at that, you're going to see us push our conservative values.” Rep. Michael Cloud (R-Texas), a member of the House Freedom Caucus, asserted voters still wanted Trump’s agenda and said he also saw Jordan as a figure who could fight any eventual impeachment effort that Democrats might bring against Trump. “He's a conservative. He's also a smart strategist. He's definitely a good communicator, and especially where we're headed with the Dems, who seem obsessed with impeachment and, you know, shenanigans, he's had to lead the defense on that before,” Cloud said. “So I think we'll be well prepared headed into the future.” Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Democratic-controlled Senate
articles.summary: Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year. During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges . But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats , and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts. "No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News. There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina. The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday. The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings. Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday. Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week. "There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee." But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule. "Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said. In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period. "The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday. But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years. "For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward." It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016. "What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary." Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year. Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so. "Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress." Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate. The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term. Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court. With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices. "Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said. articles.title: Joe Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he'd known he had cancer
articles.summary: NEED TO KNOW Joe Biden gets candid about his stage 4 prostate cancer as he releases his new memoir , Promise Me, America The former president reflects on life, withdrawing from the 2024 race and the legacy he hopes to leave Dr. Jill Biden describes the daily realities of caring for her husband with support from their family Two days after the Democrats swept the midterm elections , former President Joe Biden has that signature twinkle in his blue eyes. “Look at the people we got elected: first women governors, first Black governors,” he tells PEOPLE with a quiet rasp. At 83, and living with stage 4 prostate cancer — for which he completed radiation and is undergoing hormone therapy — Biden is slower than when he suddenly withdrew from the presidential race in 2024 following a disastrous debate against Donald Trump and amid concerns about his health. Still, his perennial optimism remains. “I’m not saying I’ll live forever,” says the one-term president, seated in the dining room of his Wilmington, Del., lake house, “but the point is that I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and I feel good.” Former President Joe Biden in his study at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will He’s fighting the disease “like hell,” Biden writes in his presidential memoir, Promise Me, America , out Nov. 17. Through it all, his wife, Dr. Jill Biden , 75, has been by his side. Being a family caregiver — like 63 million Americans — is “emotionally, physically hard,” the former first lady says after returning home from volunteering at a women’s prison, where she teaches literature part-time. Although she has help looking after her husband and says family is a constant at the house, “My days are making sure he eats right. Does he exercise? Is he taking the right medicine? Did I talk to the doctor?” Reality came into focus when she read a magazine at a nail salon and imagined traveling to the destinations on the glossy pages. “All of a sudden it struck me, like, ‘Wait a minute, this isn’t our life now,’ ” she says. “We’re on a new journey.” With no questions off the table, President Biden addresses his life and health now, his presidency and the legacy he hopes to leave behind. In May 2025, 118 days after you left office, you announced that you had been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer that had spread to your bones. You write that you’re fighting it with the “help of an incredible medical team and an even better family.” What does that fight look like? It looks very positive. There’s a lot of people who’ve been diagnosed with cancer, particularly the kind of cancer I have, who live long lives, who live for another 10, 20 years. And so far, the two tests that have been done show that the cancer is not metastasized beyond what it already was ... There are eight different pills I take a day. Former President Joe Biden at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5, 2026 Credit: Victoria Will Next June will mark your 50th wedding anniversary. What has cancer taught you about your marriage that you didn’t know before? Nothing. I knew from the beginning what she was. Jill is, first of all, bright as hell. Secondly, I think she’s the most beautiful woman in the world, which every husband probably thinks, but I believe it. And we have a real partnership. Joe Biden and wife Jill Biden pose for a photo together with their cat in May 2025. Credit: Joe Biden/X How has your family, including your grandchildren and your great-grandchild, supported you? They’re always here. “Can we come up, Pop? Pop, can we do this?” I do more with my grandchildren than I do with anybody else, and that’s for real. I’m interested and they’re interested in serious things as well ... They’re involved in a lot of things having to do with public service. They participate in a number of issues that relate to the well-being of the country. They’re the loves of my life. The Biden family celebrated Easter 2026 in Santa Ynez, California As the second Catholic to become president, you’ve been candid about how your faith has guided you through hard times. Do you still see signs of those you’ve lost? I do. I see signs of their love in their progeny. I see signs of their love of things that I find out that they have done that I didn’t know they had done before ... My son Hunter , he and his brother Beau were born a year and a day apart. They’re each other’s best friends in the world. When Beau died, it was a blow to Hunter in a way that was almost beyond repair ... Now he’s deeply involved in public policy things. He’s deeply involved in making the case, but he’s straight as an arrow in terms of his alcoholism. My dad used to have an expression: “Joey, family’s the beginning, the middle and the end.” And that’s how it is. You write, “People say I was deluding myself that I could do the job [of president] at my age. My answer to that is: I was doing the job.” Why do you think they felt that way? It’s natural. If tomorrow you’re going to say that the head of your [company] is going to be hired on as an 80-year-old person, you go, “What the hell’s going on?” But the value I think I brought was I knew so many of the leaders, I knew their inclinations, I knew what was going on, and many of them came to me. I thought it was value added, not subtracted. Standard medical guidelines don’t recommend routine prostate cancer screenings for men over 70. You write, “I was treated no differently from any other 82-year-old man in America. Maybe I should have been.” What do you say to Americans who believe that a screening should have been part of your annual physical? Look, White House doctors are doing what the whole entire medical profession is doing ... I had some discomfort, and Jill thought, Why isn’t that test done for men who are in their 70s? And there wasn’t any particular [sign] except recurring pain. When he wasn’t downing a black-and-white milkshake, former President Joe Biden chatted with diners at the Charcoal Pit in Wilmington, Del., his favorite diner since high school, on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will You describe a “cynical twist” on your cancer news: that some folks said you hid your cancer as president. Why do you think they reacted that way? A lot of people do that. They hide bad news from the public if they’re elected officials. I didn’t do that. We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it’s important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn’t hiding it at all. Many have spoken about the toll of the Presidency. How might your undiagnosed cancer have exacerbated that? First of all, I never felt the toll. I read [others] like Harry Truman talk about [how] it’s the most difficult job in the world. I didn’t find it that way. And so I, quite frankly, found that it didn’t in any way interfere with my job. Former President Joe Biden in his study at home in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5 Credit: Victoria Will What do you miss the most about the job? The staff, the people in the White House. They’re good people, from the people making sure there’s a sheet on the bed to the people who are taking care of all the visitors that come through. They all have a sense of honor, what they’re doing in the White House. It’s the People’s House. What’s your reaction to the Trump ballroom and the East Wing being destroyed? Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office. I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing ... I’ve viewed the president’s judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: “I built that.” I find it beneath the country. After Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris in 2024, he and Melania returned to the White House on Jan. 20, 2025. Credit: Jim WATSON/AFP/Getty It’s been two years and four months since that debate moment on the stage with Trump. What is your perspective on it now? Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate. To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential. Former President Joe Biden chatted with staff at the Charcoal Pit, his favorite diner since high school, in Wilmington, Del., on Nov. 5. Credit: Victoria Will In hindsight, looking at the 2024 election, is there anything you would’ve done differently? What I can’t say, because there’s no evidence of it — if I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]. But that wasn’t the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job. Hunter has been speaking out on podcasts and social media. What do you make of that? Hunter is one of the brightest men I know. He has more moral and physical courage than most people I know, and I’m really proud of him. He’s making the case as to how we should proceed as a country. He’s said of the pardon you gave him: “Was it good for our Constitution? Was it good for the American people? Was it good for my father’s legacy? No on all accounts.” What’s your perspective? I disagree ... I watched the modus operandi of Trump. He goes after people without any basis, whether they’re viewed as an enemy. I knew what he would do. If I hadn’t pardoned — not just some of my family members, anyone who’s dealt with me—he would go back and try to do harm to them, as I’ve observed. Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE’s free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. In your book, for the first time, you share the letter that Trump left you in the Oval Office after you beat him in the 2020 election. Your takeaway: “It was almost as if there were two Donald Trumps.” What do you mean? That could have been written by President Kennedy to me or by President Johnson or by George Bush. I mean, it was gracious, it was generous, and it was totally inconsistent with the kind of president he’d been. Joe Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America,” out Nov. 17 You write, “Promise me, America, that we will be the nation we know in our hearts we can be and should be.” What does that nation mean to you at 83, after more than 50 years of public service? It means to continue to hold those truths to be self-evident, that we’re all created equal. I got involved in politics because of the Civil Rights movement. It means to be engaged in trying to help make the country a better place than it has been, to give people the benefit of the doubt ... When I say, “Promise me, America,” I mean, America, you know the promises we made. Let’s keep them. Joe Biden was sworn in on his family Bible when he became president on Jan. 20, 2021. Credit: Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times/Getty How do you want the American people to remember you? I tell you, it’s the greatest honor any man or woman could be given anywhere to be the President of the United States of America. And I hope I kept the promise of America ... I didn’t say I didn’t make mistakes—but I meant what I said, and I did what I said I was going to do. articles.title: A 67-year-old Democratic veteran is becoming the left's favorite to replace Schumer
articles.summary: Progressive lawmakers and activists are hoping to harness momentum from last week’s sweeping Democratic victories to install inspiring new congressional leaders. Many have looked at the Senate and found their guy: a 67-year-old father of three from an affluent Washington suburb who has held public office continuously since 1991. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has emerged as the alternative of choice for a swath of Democrats who believe Chuck Schumer, the longtime Senate Democratic leader, should step aside despite presiding over massive midterm gains. It’s the culmination of a remarkable resurgence for Van Hollen, who spent years inching up the Democratic leadership ladder in the House only to ditch his seniority there for the back benches of the Senate in 2017. Over the past two years, he has emerged as an increasingly strident critic of the Democratic party establishment and its approach to President Donald Trump, as well as its positions on populist economic policies and the U.S. relationship with Israel — and members of the party’s left flank have noticed. A wave of House Democrats, outside activists and even at least one newly elected senator are effectively trying to draft him into what could be an uphill race to unseat the 75-year-old Schumer as majority leader. “I have been very impressed by Senator Van Hollen’s leadership,” said Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who beat a more centrist Democrat in her state’s primary and has said she will not back Schumer. Van Hollen has wavered on whether he is pursuing a role in Senate leadership or perhaps instead a 2028 run for the presidency. He said Tuesday he is “actively listening” as he keeps the door open to a majority leader bid ahead of the early December caucus elections. “I’m trying to talk to our members, and I think it’s important to reach out to everybody,” he said in the Capitol halls. Flanagan said she had not had “formal conversations” with Van Hollen, but another younger Democrat — Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan — met with him this week as she called for a leadership shakeup. Outside the building, at a gathering of progressive groups charting an agenda for the coming Democratic majorities, Van Hollen was sharply critical of the existing Senate Democratic power structure — and Schumer in particular. “We just saw democracy in America in action — we should bring a little more democracy to the United States Senate,” he said, before later accusing Schumer and the Senate Democratic campaign arm of having “sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC” to oppose more progressive candidates in this year’s primaries. That outspokenness has gotten Van Hollen noticed on the left — and it has been especially striking coming from a son of prominent U.S. diplomats who spent decades dutifully rising through the Democratic Party establishment and chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees. “Van Hollen represents a bridge between the old guard — people who’ve been in office for a long time with a more moderate orientation — and the new generation that is coming into office,” said Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution. His rhetoric and actions have evolved dramatically, however, since Trump returned to office in 2025. The administration’s spending cuts decimated Van Hollen’s constituency — particularly in his political base of Montgomery County — and his posts on the Appropriations and Foreign Relations committees gave him a front-row seat to Trump’s elimination of USAID. Meanwhile, he became an outspoken critic of the White House’s mass deportation agenda and was the first U.S. lawmaker to visit the El Salvador prison where the administration was sending scores of deportees — including a Maryland man, Kilmar Ábrego García, who had been mistakenly deported in contravention of a court order. Van Hollen has also become increasingly critical of the U.S. posture toward Israel, joining early Democratic pushes to restrict arms sales to Benjamin Netanyahu’s government as its war on Gaza after the 2023 Hamas attacks grew increasingly brutal. “He’s been correct,” said Jeff Cohen, founder of RootsAction, a group pushing its members to back Van Hollen over Schumer. “He’s been with the base of the party on most issues: redefining the U.S.-Israel relationship is one. Taxing the wealthy is another, standing up to AI — all of these issues that Schumer is wrong on.” Van Hollen’s approach to the Senate leadership race has evolved in recent days. He downplayed a bid for top leader earlier this year, including saying in a recent interview that it has “not been my focus.” The day after the election, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed appeared to believe he had passed on a run, calling Van Hollen “my white whale” in response to a question about his ideal Senate leader. But asked about the matter Tuesday as the drumbeat for his candidacy grew, Van Hollen said there should not be a “coronation” for Schumer as he described his ongoing listening tour. “We should not support anybody for leader without a very clear plan and as you know, there are many people who think that a change is required,” he said. A Senate aide who was granted anonymity to describe Van Hollen’s thinking said the senator has been influenced by the scale of his party’s midterm victory and the calls he has heard for change — as well as the public outreach he is getting. The aide said Van Hollen is not coordinating the outside effort to nudge him into challenging Schumer. Senate Democrats still broadly expect Schumer to be reelected as leader, and some are openly warning Van Hollen away from jumping into the race. “I'm going to vote for Schumer. He helped recruit a great class, and I can't imagine why you would vote for someone like Van Hollen with no record of doing anything,” pro-Israel Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) told reporters. Asked about whether Van Hollen will run, Fetterman added, “I dare him to.” Schumer’s backers point to his decades of fundraising experience, deep well of relationships within the caucus and across the party, and his work to unite his colleagues and battle Trump over the past year. And with Democrats poised to pick up as many as nine seats — a once-unthinkable outcome — they are questioning why senators would depose the leader who helped make it happen. "When the manager takes you to the World Series, you give him another contract,” Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) said Tuesday at a joint news conference with Schumer. But those arguments are carrying little water with those who view Schumer as out of touch with the direction of the party. They note that while he supported the incoming freshmen with hundreds of millions of dollars of general-election spending, he opposed some of them during the primary. Van Hollen could be using his flirtations with a bid to influence some end-of-year decisionmaking. He is pushing Congress to cut off Iran war funding as they head toward a Dec. 11 government funding deadline, and he wants a provision mandating cooperation with Israel stripped from the annual defense policy bill. Those stances could help push Schumer and the party into a more confrontational posture, which Van Hollen signaled he wanted in an interview earlier this year. “It’s going to be very important that Democrats let voters know not only what we’re against but what we stand for,” he said. “And I think a lot of voters, you know, think Democrats have been too much finger-in-the-wind. They’ve been too wishy-washy.” Grace Yarrow and Lisa Kashinsky contributed to this report. articles.title: Military-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite U.S. blacklist
articles.summary: By Eduardo Baptista BEIJING, Nov 11 (Reuters) - A Chinese university with deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales ‌of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. ‌But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation. Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight ​of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defense" group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to ‌H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity ⁠from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. TRADE BLACKLIST Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related ⁠to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of ​26 ​Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services ​that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China's defence industry ‌or military research. The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment. NVIDIA CHIPS FOR MILITARY-LINKED RESEARCH US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each.  The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's ‌procurement records. In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and ​fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers ​operated. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing ​contracts. A WIDER MARKET The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the ‌US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an ​H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips ​in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of ​Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate ‌January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro ​Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 ​chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/news/exclusive-pla-linked-chinese-university-051308504.html

articles.title: Alina Habba Mildon fired from company that gave her $50 million deal before Trump pardon
articles.summary: Alina Habba Mildon , a former attorney for President Donald Trump , has been terminated from her multi-million-dollar role at Florida-registered Concord Partners following months of intense public scrutiny, according to reports. In a November 4 termination letter obtained by The New York Times , Concord Partners — a firm established by the family of Venezuelan billionaire banker Julio Herrera Velutini — cited a "failure to perform duties" as the reason for releasing  Mildon. A source close to the family told the publication that Mildon’s attention shifted away from her role after she began dating Turkish investor Turhan Mildon earlier this year. The departure follows public criticism from Trump, who denounced the lucrative arrangement after details of the contract were disclosed. "I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters last month, according to The New York Times . "I told her, and I said, I don’t want her paid.' I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that. And it was far too much." Mediaite also reported Trump saying of the arrangement: "You know, it’s one thing for a person to get paid legal fees or whatever — she’s a lawyer. I thought it was a totally obnoxious and outrageous and it’s not acceptable. Not acceptable, at all." Alina Habba Mildon, a former lawyer for President Donald Trump, has been fired from her multi-million dollar position at Florida-registered Concord Partners following months of heavy media coverage, according to reports (Getty Images) Following media coverage of the contract, Trump told aides and allies that the Herrera family should withhold payments to Mildon, suggesting she make a donation to his future presidential library or another entity. When asked by CBS News about the possibility of donating to the library, Mildon responded via text with "haha" before quickly deleting the message, according to Mediaite . Despite her firing, Mildon will retain an $8 million signing bonus and $6.5 million in payments already received. The original four-year agreement, which began on January 1 when she was brought on as general counsel, was structured to pay her $10 million annually plus additional bonuses. Mildon was serving as a special government employee and senior adviser to the attorney general when she joined Concord Partners. Special government employee status permits individuals to serve the federal government for up to 130 days while retaining outside employment, subject to conflict-of-interest guidelines. The move follows public condemnation from Trump, who called the lucrative arrangement ‘obnoxious’ and urged the Florida firm to stop paying his former lawyer (Getty Images) The hiring occurred shortly after Herrera reached a plea agreement in August 2025 that reduced his federal charges — originally related to an alleged 2022 scheme to bribe the governor of Puerto Rico — down to a single misdemeanor campaign finance violation. Around the same time, Herrera's daughter, Isabela Herrera, donated $3.5 million to a super PAC aligned with Trump. Weeks after Concord Partners hired Mildon, Trump granted Herrera a full and unconditional pardon . Mildon has consistently denied that her employment had any connection to the pardon. "Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false," Mildon said in a statement previously reported by The New York Times . A person close to Mildon said she intends to pursue legal action over the termination. Despite her abrupt departure, Mildon will keep $14.5 million in payments and signing bonuses from the four-year agreement (Getty Images) The termination comes after a series of setbacks for the couple following their September wedding in New York. The New York Times reported recently that Turhan Mildon gave misleading or exaggerated accounts of his age, past marriages, foreign contacts and business operations. Additionally, Turhan Mildon remains central to a White House inquiry initiated after Mildon accused former Trump administration official Richard Grenell of skimming funds from a donation made by her husband. Upon investigating the claims at Trump's directive, White House officials determined that the $17.6 million in question originated from a government account in the Democratic Republic of Congo — where Turhan Mildon holds business contracts — rather than from Turhan Mildon's personal funds, as reported by The New York Times . articles.title: JFK's family sues Trump over arch they say would cast a shadow on late president's grave
articles.summary: Several members of the Kennedy family have sued President Donald Trump , aiming to stop the building of the triumphal arch he hopes to build near Washington, D.C., new court filings show. The proposed 250-foot monument in the style of Paris’ Arc de Triomphe would be built on the Virginia side of the Potomac River between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, where American veterans have been laid to rest since the Civil War. According to Kennedy family members behind the lawsuit, the 25-story arch would "cast a shadow" over memorials to their family members laid to rest in the historic burial site. "President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch," says the Kennedy family members’  lawsuit, "that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes." According to the lawsuit, the arch would block sightlines onto the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, a memorial to the former president who was assassinated in 1963 . They contend it will also cast a shadow over the graves of prominent Kennedys buried in the cemetery. In addition to JFK, others buried there include Robert F. Kennedy, the former senator assassinated in 1968 , and Sen. Edward "Ted" Kennedy, who died in 2009 after 43 years of serving in Congress. Among the nine Kennedys named as plaintiffs in the lawsuit are RFK’s daughter Kerry Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, Jr. "Vanity should never stand in the way of valor," Kerry Kennedy, president of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, said in a statement following the court filing in Washington, D.C. A White House spokesperson in a statement slammed efforts to block construction of "this magnificent Arch." "It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." USA TODAY has reached out to Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for comment. Trump has previously promoted the project as both a landmark and a military asset. Speaking on Nov. 2 during an event highlighting improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, he said the arch could house drones and snipers. "It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said. The court filing is the latest attempt to thwart the president’s attempt to build the arch. Opponents have previously argued that the arch would obstruct the view from the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington Cemetery, which was built on the confiscated land of former Confederate General Robert E. Lee. The clear view between the two sites is meant to represent the reunification of the country following the Civil War, according to court filings. Plans to build Trump’s arch have been approved by a board led by people appointed by the president. But other hurdles remain. A federal judge on Nov. 5 temporarily blocked the project from going forward in response to a separate lawsuit brought by Washington and Virginia, arguing that the president needs approval from Congress in order to build. Trump's plans to remake the nation's capital, including the proposed arch, are not popular among Americans. In May, polls showed 52% of Americans were against the project, including 41% who strongly oppose it, while only 21% of people support the plan to build the towering arch. Democrats retaking Congress in the midterms argued in the run-up to the election that the president was too focused on construction projects in Washington and not focused enough on bringing down the cost of living for everyday Americans. "I don't know if you've noticed, but he is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV," former President Barack Obama quipped in one viral campaign moment. "Guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House, paved over the Rose Garden – paved it over – put a helicopter pad on the side lawn." articles.title: Democratic lawmakers seek information on 8-year-old Haitian boy taken into ICE custody
articles.summary: A group of Democratic lawmakers is seeking information from the Trump administration after an 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken into government custody last week. In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Tuesday, six Democratic lawmakers asked what steps are being taken to reunite the child with his family. "Video footage appears to show the use of restraints on a child who seemed to pose no threat to those around him, raising serious questions about the handling of this incident," the lawmakers wrote. "We express concerns about the basis for this action and the harm it may cause a young child who appeared for his required hearing." Trump says 'too tough' deportation policies hurt him in the midterms The 8-year-old, who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year as part of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown , was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in last week, according to local advocates and school officials. The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was detained alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday. Advocates and school officials previously said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year. "They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance. STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ice Police agents - Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Close-up of POLICE ICE marking on the back of worn by a trio of DHS police officers at the scene of an incident. A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News that agents acted under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship. "Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said. Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings." "The effects of this action extend far beyond one child and his family," the lawmakers said in their letter. articles.title: 沙特10月石油产量飙升26%，创战争爆发以来最高，布伦特原油本月跌逾两成
articles.summary: 沙特阿拉伯石油产量大幅反弹，带动波斯湾地区供应全面恢复，正在加速拖累全球油价。 据彭博获得的石油输出国组织（OPEC）秘书处月报显示，沙特10月日均原油产量升至1056万桶，较上月激增26%，创战争爆发以来最高水平。 与此同时，伊拉克产量也攀升至战时新高。大量原油涌入实货市场，在需求依然疲软的背景下压低了价差，市场出现供过于求的初步迹象。 此轮增产恰逢OPEC评估各成员国最大产能的关键节点，该评估结果将于11月29日的OPEC+在线会议上被用于商讨2027年产量目标。 沙特阿美首席执行官Amin Nasser上周在阿布扎比行业会议上表示，公司目标是"在第四季度最大化产量"，并指出库存补充将显著提振全球需求。 布伦特原油期货本月已累计下跌约21%，目前报每桶93美元。 沙特产量逼近战前峰值，霍尔木兹海峡运输突破是关键 沙特10月日产量1056万桶，仅比战争爆发前的2月产量低数十万桶，略高于该国在OPEC框架内的配额上限。 产量回升的核心驱动力在于运输瓶颈的突破。沙特已在相当程度上掌握了通过霍尔木兹海峡进行秘密穿梭运输的技术，这一策略由阿联酋在战争早期率先摸索推行。 与此同时，沙特还得以启用一条通往红海沿岸的替代管道——尽管该管道此前曾遭受袭击。 伊拉克方面同样向OPEC报告，10月日产量升至约490万桶的战时新高，明显超出其商定的产量上限。 实际产量与配额核查存在出入，OPEC立场仍不明朗 值得注意的是，OPEC在评估成员国配额执行情况时，采用外部来源数据而非成员国自行申报数字，两组数据之间存在显著差异。 依据外部来源数据，伊拉克10月实际日产量约为449.1万桶，基本符合其规定限额；沙特的外部来源数据则为日均919.4万桶，仍明显低于其配额上限。这与沙特自报的1056万桶存在较大差距。 鉴于战争期间众多成员国被迫长期大幅低于配额生产，导致全球石油库存骤降，OPEC对于配额违规问题将采取何种立场目前尚不明确。 此番产量大增，也为OPEC+此前在冲突期间通过的一系列配额上调决定提供了事后注脚。彼时受出口中断拖累，这些上调几乎形同虚设，但当前正好赋予产油国打开阀门的额外空间。 OPEC+对各成员国最大产能的审核预计将在未来数日内完成，届时全联盟将于11月29日召开在线会议，以此为基础商议2027年的产量目标安排。 市场份额竞争加剧，沙特与阿联酋竞相下调面向亚洲售价 产量回升的背后，市场份额之争也在悄然升温。阿联酋今年5月在长期成员资格后选择退出OPEC，以摆脱产量上限约束，自主参与市场竞争。 近期，沙特与阿联酋均大幅下调了面向亚洲买家的12月船货官方售价，竞争态势趋于激烈。 此轮价格战信号，叠加供应端持续恢复，令市场对未来油价走势愈发审慎。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 大摩警告：旧存储价格正在见顶，2028年供需或转向宽松
articles.summary: 旧存储芯片市场的定价红利正逐步走向终结。摩根士丹利在最新报告中警告，云端资本支出不确定性上升、消费端需求持续疲软，以及供需关系料将于2028年前后趋于平衡，旧存储行业的盈利逻辑已从"向上弹性"转向"向下防御"。 据追风交易台，摩根士丹利发布报告指出， 美国中期选举后，预计2028年美国数据中心约20%的新增容量将推迟至2029年落地，涉及约5吉瓦的建设规模，相当于全球2028年新增容量的10%。 这一延迟可能在2028年为科技供应链制造"断层"，压缩旧存储芯片的定价空间，并引发库存积压风险。 与此同时，摩根士丹利对SLC NAND、MLC NAND、NOR及DDR4四大产品的供需模型进行更新后发现，各细分市场均呈现趋于平衡的态势，尤其以2028年为甚。 报告对市场的直接影响已经显现：摩根士丹利下调了多只旧存储相关个股的评级，并大幅削减目标价，同时下调2027至2028年盈利预期。分析师将1.0倍市净率（P/B）作为估值下行锚，而非以盈利高峰作为支撑底部，标志着市场对该板块的定价逻辑出现系统性转变。 定价优势成"双刃剑"，需求走弱暴露脆弱性 摩根士丹利此前的建仓逻辑建立在旧存储芯片的差异化定价能力上——相较于主流存储， 旧存储受固定价格长期协议约束较少，因此在短缺周期中能更快速地提价。然而，该行现在认为，这种灵活性正在演变为双向风险。 报告指出，云端支出可见度正在下滑，企业端增量需求的确定性随之减弱；与此同时，消费端需求大幅走软，终端客户承接进一步涨价的能力受到明显制约。 摩根士丹利的PC半导体研究显示，2026年一季度至三季度出现了集中采购的"拉货"现象，但四季度随即进入更深度的库存消化阶段， 表明此前的订单规模高于实际消费需求，存在透支之嫌。 报告特别说明， 上述分析仅针对旧存储领域，包括DDR3/4、SLC/MLC NAND及NOR闪存，不涉及全球主流DDR5或TLC/QLC NAND市场。 供需模型更新：短缺窗口正在收窄 摩根士丹利对SLC NAND、MLC NAND、NOR及DDR4的最新供需模型均指向同一趋势：供需缺口逐步收窄，2028年前后或实现基本平衡乃至出现过剩。 具体预测显示， 2028年SLC NAND、MLC NAND和NOR的供需缺口分别约为-3%、-5%和-1%，而DDR4则可能出现约+1%的供给过剩。 分析师指出，近期短缺局面未必会立即消散，但缺口收窄本身足以削弱增量定价能力，并早于盈利高点触发股价重估。 基于此，摩根士丹利下调了对多个产品线2027至2028年的ASP假设：NOR及DDR4的ASP预测在2028年四季度分别被削减约23%至26%；部分公司的SLC NAND ASP预测降幅则更为显著。 在出货量预测基本不变的情况下，收入和毛利率估算随之下移，2028年EPS预测普遍被下调10%至30%以上。 数据中心资本支出延迟：2028年供应链"气穴"风险 美国中期选举后出台的数据中心新立法是此轮预期转变的重要触发因素。 据摩根士丹利美国团队测算， 德克萨斯州和俄亥俄州等地的立法变化导致约5吉瓦的数据中心建设从2028年推迟至2029年，这意味着美国2028年数据中心新增容量将同比下降约4%，2029年则将大幅反弹约38%。 在全球层面，摩根士丹利现预计2028年全球数据中心新增容量同比增长约9%，2029年则升至约20%。 这一"前低后高"的节奏对旧存储行业构成阶段性压力——需求延迟叠加供给持续爬坡， 2028年极可能形成阶段性供大于求的局面，届时库存周期风险将显著上升。 值得关注的是， 摩根士丹利维持对全球超大规模云厂商资本支出的总量预测不变， 预计2027年约1.6万亿美元、2028年约1.8万亿美元，但明确指出若建设进度进一步推迟，2028年的预测存在下行偏差风险。 估值框架转向：以账面价值为下行锚 面对盈利预期的系统性下修，摩根士丹利将估值方法论调整为以1.0倍市净率作为下行估值锚，取代此前以盈利高峰作为估值底部的框架。 分析师认为，对于资本密集型IDM及晶圆代工企业而言，账面价值在周期性低谷中具有心理支撑意义——当盈利暂时承压时，投资者通常会更多地回归净资产基础进行估值。 在各细分公司层面，目标价调整幅度相当显著，但IDM类企业与无晶圆厂（Fabless）设计公司之间的处理方式有所区别。 报告明确指出，1.0倍P/B的框架主要适用于IDM/晶圆代工类企业，对Fabless公司并不适用同一估值方法论，因为后者缺乏资产负债表层面的估值地板支撑，在周期下行中面临更高的波动风险。 分析师将价格放缓、订单削减及库存消化列为主要下行催化剂；云端订单需求重新走强，或供给扩张进度延迟，则是当前情境下最主要的上行风险。 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 以上精彩内容来自 追风交易台 articles.title: 美10月核心CPI超预期，美国数据中心成政治焦点，国内传统行业加快出清---1111宏观脱水
articles.summary: 美国10月整体与核心CPI均超预期强劲，核心CPI环比连续三个月维持0.3%，通胀广泛性提升。家具与医疗商品、超级核心服务偏强。数据公布后美债短长端收益率同步上行，12月加息概率升至90.9%，12月加息基本无悬念但25BP或仍是基准假设。 限制数据中心已成两党共识，社区成本成为新监管重点。德州政策收紧方向明确但落地方式仍存不确定性。2027年投资受影响相对有限，2028年新增建设需重新评估。建设成本将从社区转向开发商，开发模式趋近配套开发。 国内市场担忧集中于AI降温与贸易摩擦导致外需走弱、债务周期与就业环境压制消费需求。被忽视的积极信号是传统领域正在加快出清，社会集团消费修复基础正在形成。2027年建议关注供给侧三条主线与扩内需政策内涵变化。

articles.title: 王毅同美国国务卿鲁比奥通电话
articles.summary:
中共中央政治局委员、外交部长王毅11日同美国国务卿鲁比奥通电话。双方就中美关系及两国元首互动深入交换意见，通话是积极和建设性的。
王毅表示，中美关系稳定势头来之不易，是两个大国从各自和共同利益出发作出的理性选择。中国对美政策保持稳定性和连续性，愿同美方加强沟通合作，妥善处理分歧和敏感问题，相互支持办好2026年亚太经合组织领导人非正式会议和二十国集团领导人峰会，推动中美建设性战略稳定关系落地见效。（新华社） 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 反数据中心浪潮下，AI交易还能走多远？关键看GPU租赁价格
articles.summary: 数据中心的政治逆风正在重塑AI投资逻辑，但这场交易的生死，最终取决于一个鲜少被关注的价格信号——GPU租赁价格。 据彭博宏观策略师Simon White撰文指出，美国中期选举后，算力供给面临收紧风险，市场已率先作出反应。上周市场急剧下挫后虽有所企稳，但波动尚未平息。核心问题在于： 若数据中心建设受阻，GPU租赁价格能否通过上涨，足以弥补资本开支萎缩带来的损失？ 从市场已有的价格信号看，答案具有一定可行性。这一逻辑的成立，将驱动AI交易内部发生结构性轮动——从依赖持续扩张的AI实验室、新兴云服务商和数据中心建设链，转向坐拥大量存量算力的超大规模云厂商（hyperscalers）。 选举冲击：算力供给收紧的政治根源 民主党在中期选举中取得压倒性胜利，计算资源可能面临趋紧。多个选区的选举实质上演变为针对AI的公投，民主党得票率涨幅最大的州，恰恰是数据中心布局最为密集的地区。 然而，竞选口号与执政现实之间历来存在落差。数据中心对经济举足轻重，民主党究竟会在多大力度上收紧相关项目审批，仍有待观察。 市场并未等待答案。上周的急跌之后，虽有所回稳，但鉴于全球第二大市值公司深陷间谍丑闻，加之波动率控制基金仍需降低风险敞口以应对更高波动，企稳能否持续仍是未知数。 GPU租赁价格：判断AI交易成色的核心指标 彭博宏观策略师Simon White指出， 待市场情绪沉淀后，投资者需密切追踪GPU租赁价格走势——这是判断算力供给是否相对需求收缩、进而衡量AI交易演变方向的关键指标。 目前，选举后GPU租赁价格的上行趋势尚无明显变化。但若数据中心新建项目遭到叫停或审批推迟，租赁价格有可能加速攀升。 这将从根本上改变AI交易的经济学逻辑： 有利于已拥有大规模存量算力的超大规模云厂商，而不利于实质上处于算力"空头"状态的AI实验室和新兴云服务商，同样不利于数据中心的建设方、设备供应商和电力提供商——包括英伟达、Eaton和Vertiv。 自选举以来，超大规模云厂商股价已出现反弹，而新兴云服务商、电力供应商和半导体股票则普遍走低，这一分化印证了上述逻辑。 供给冲击有多大？数据中心中断风险测算 数据中心建设受阻的潜在规模不可小觑。能源研究机构Modo Energy在中期选举后的评估报告中估算，已宣布的数据中心项目中，约40%可能受到暂停令冲击，涉及算力容量高达256吉瓦。 不过，该机构同时认为，到2035年，算力负荷增长仅会温和下滑——部分项目延期后仍将推进，另一些则会迁往政策更友好的地区，无论是美国其他州还是海外市场。Modo Energy的测算显示，到2035年，净减少的算力容量约为4吉瓦，而其估算的规划总量超过600吉瓦；德克萨斯州（ERCOT电网）的缺口预计基本可在其他地区得到弥补。 当然，预测本身存在误差，即便整体影响有限，也不排除短期出现局部算力瓶颈，从而推高GPU租赁价格。 资本开支与租赁价格：能否形成对冲？ 投资者面临的核心问题是：若数据中心管控导致资本开支收缩，算力价格的上涨能否充分弥补损失？ 粗略测算表明，这一逻辑在数学上具有可行性。Epoch AI的数据显示，每吉瓦数据中心的总资本开支约为370亿美元，按两年建设周期折算，年均投入约185亿美元。而CoreWeave目前的算力租赁年化收入约为每吉瓦400亿美元。若GPU租赁价格上涨30%（英伟达H100芯片租赁价格过去一年已上涨逾50%），每年可额外带来约120亿美元收入。 据此，1.5吉瓦存量算力实现30%的价格上浮，即可覆盖1吉瓦新增算力的资本开支损失。 考虑到美国现有约30吉瓦的算力装机量，若其中10%至20%能够快速重新定价，经济学逻辑便会从"建设新算力"转向"变现存量算力"。 验证这一逻辑是否成立的反向信号明确：若资本开支与GPU租赁价格同步下滑，则论断有误。否则，AI交易最坏的结果或许只是内部的结构性轮动。即便Anthropic和OpenAI因算力不足而推迟IPO，市场也未必无法消化，因为部分经济利益已向超大规模云厂商集中。 市场近期企稳：对冲基金去杠杆提供缓冲 从短期维度看，有两个理由支持市场在近期波动后趋于稳定。 据Goldman Sachs数据，作为上周抛售主力的对冲基金已完成相当程度的去杠杆：过去一周，整体头寸规模下降近9个百分点，经贝塔调整后的风险敞口下降近16个百分点。Morgan Stanley则指出，对冲基金净风险敞口已降至一年低位。高杠杆、高同质化的持仓结构，使对冲基金容易触发局部踩踏，但受约束较少、决策节奏更慢的零售和机构投资者尚未大规模跟进抛售——杠杆ETF资金流向显示，散户卖盘尚不明显；机构方面，在未经投资委员会审议前，全面退出的可能性亦较低，且机构对科技股的持仓比例依然较高。 其次，当前经济衰退信号并不明显。宏观数据显示，股市大幅深跌（跌幅超过20%）通常发生于经济衰退期间，而目前并无此类迹象。 轮动而非终结：AI交易的演变路径 大规模取消数据中心项目将对经济造成重创，但这并非基准情形。正如上文分析，大量项目可迁往政策环境更为友好的地区。 更可能的结果是AI交易内部的结构性轮动：超大规模云厂商因存量算力的稀缺性溢价而受益，而AI实验室、新兴云服务商及数据中心建设链则承压。这种轮动会削弱AI交易的广度与活力，却也可能在更窄、更脆弱的形态下延续这场交易。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 美银之后，大摩也将英伟达移除“首选股”名单！
articles.summary: 英伟达正面临华尔街顶级机构的信心动摇。 继美国银行之后，摩根士丹利周三也将英伟达从其半导体板块"首选股"名单中移除，尽管两家机构均维持"增持"或"买入"评级。 这一连串降级动作，折射出华黄仁勋个人丑闻对英伟达投资逻辑的冲击正在蔓延。 摩根士丹利分析师在周三的研报中指出， 黄仁勋的领导力对英伟达的战略方向"至关重要"，而当前围绕其个人的不确定性已令风险收益比趋于不利。 此前，英伟达股价在周一和周二连续两日分别下跌4.3%和5.47%，两日累计跌幅接近10%，本周市值蒸发约4700亿美元。周三美股盘前，股价有所反弹，涨幅最高超过5%。 美国银行则早一步于11月10日将英伟达、美光科技（Micron Technology）及泛林集团（Lam Research）同时移出其"US 1精选名单"，但对三家公司均维持"买入"评级。美银分析师Vivek Arya在研报中列出三种情景：一是影响可控、领导层保持稳定；二是不确定性持续压制估值；三是领导层出现变动或监管限制收紧，届时将需要重新评估盈利预期。 据CNBC报道，黄仁勋周一已返回公司办公室，试图传递"一切如常"的信号，并于周二继续在办公室主持会议，为11月17日的季度财报做准备。然而，市场对于其风波可能引发的连锁反应仍保持高度警惕。 大摩态度急转，距重新纳入不足六周 摩根士丹利此次移除英伟达的决定，时间节点颇为微妙。 就在约六周前的10月2日， 该行分析师Joseph Moore刚刚将英伟达重新纳入半导体板块首选股名单，彼时他在完成与公司管理层的路演后写道，"我们认同并将该股重新列为半导体板块首选"。 就在本周风波升级前的11月9日， 摩根士丹利半导体团队仍将英伟达保留在首选名单之上，并将当时的板块抛售定性为"似乎过度"。然而短短两日之内，黄仁勋丑闻的持续深化令该行迅速改变立场。 自10月2日被纳入首选名单以来，英伟达股价已累计下跌逾25%，目前较10月6日的历史收盘高点低约28%。富国银行分析师Aaron Rakers虽于周二维持"增持"评级，但将目标价从315美元下调至300美元。 机构降级背后：评级与精选名单的区别 值得注意的是，美银和摩根士丹利均未下调英伟达的投资评级，仅将其移出各自的高信念精选名单。这一区别具有实质意义。 以美银为例，"买入"评级仅代表分析师预期股票将产生正向总回报，而"US 1精选名单"则是分析师以声誉背书的高确信度投资组合。 将股票移出该名单，意味着分析师认为近期风险收益比已不够吸引，即便长期AI叙事逻辑依然成立。 对于被动投资者而言，英伟达的持续承压同样值得关注。在VanEck半导体ETF（SMH）中，英伟达权重约为20.5%至20.8%，美光和泛林合计约占8%至9%，三者合计占该基金约28%至29%的权重。若机构资金持续轮出上述标的，被动基金的资金流出压力或将对散户投资组合产生显著影响。 11月17日财报成关键节点 当前，市场目光已转向11月17日英伟达季度财报。这将是风波爆发后公司首次公开披露业绩，也是投资者评估事件对基本面实际影响的重要窗口。 美银分析师Vivek Arya所列出的三种情景中，最为悲观的一种涉及调查出现不利发现、领导层出现变动，或监管层面收紧限制，届时市场将不得不重新评估英伟达的盈利预期。目前，英伟达股价仍处于历史高点下方约28%的位置，而华尔街两大顶级机构相继撤出精选名单的信号，令这场不确定性的边界更加难以厘清。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 东财陈果：A股半导体或已计入28年悲观预期，AI应用关注局部突破
articles.summary: 6月做客华尔街见闻 「大咖会客厅」 时，陈果提醒，需警惕市场对AI预期偏高、硅基上游拥挤度过高，可考虑配置再平衡，积极关注其他方向机会。 五个多月后，相关板块经历明显调整，他的关注点也转向：市场是否可能已计入偏悲观预期？ 11月10日，东方财富证券研究所副所长、首席策略官陈果再次做客 「大咖会客厅」 ，围绕AI行情、行业机会及年末市场展望展开交流。 在他看来，对AI资本开支回报及持续性的担忧一直存在，担忧在下半年边际增加有其合理性，但因为6月股价上涨而高估AI产业趋势和因为过去几个月股价下跌而判断AI泡沫破灭一样，条件并不充分。 他指出，A股在几个月内对AI硬件的态度发生了近乎180度的转变，半导体板块股价可能已提前计入2028年AI Capex的悲观预期，而现实是大型云厂商未明确改变对2027和2028年CAPEX的态度，很难说一定会显著下修，而2028年之后的AI商业化与CAPEX增速会如何更是看不清，市场短期存在超跌。 他认为，从当前到明年初，市场仍处于一个相对有利的时间窗口，但反弹可能伴随反复，需要持续观察海外利率与油价、云厂商资本开支以及国内政策的变化。直播回放→ 全球市场风云变幻，年末配置何去何从？ 核心观点速览： 担心美国AI Capex 下修有合理性，但判断AI泡沫破灭，条件并不充分。 自由现金流承压和利率高企，依然不等于云厂商一定会立即大幅削减资本开支。 28 年之后谁也说不准 ， 短期先关注超跌修复机会，AI硬件也有望参与反弹。 A股对AI的定价可能已提前反映了对2028年及之后的担忧，但产业发展可能有变数。 美国AI 基建因为体量已较大，在28年之后要谈整体增速与成长性确实越来越难，也越来越需要AI商业化支撑。后续AI应用可以先看局部突破。 AI制药、端侧AI、机器人等领域的边际进展，可能形成投资线索，但这个阶段需要产业思维的耐心资本。 中期选举结果验证 “ 科技以人为本”，硅基不能自顾自激进扩张，更不能与民争利，还是要让碳基充分感受到对其收入及生活的实质改善。 AI需要将“AI-”变为“AI+”。 市场的“审美”会比6月更加多元。抱团思维散去，A股市场也会更加理性审视投资价值，既有资金关心短期景气爆发力和市值想象空间，也会有资金重视自由现金流、竞争壁垒和市值下限 。他也关注医药、部分周期及稳定增长类公司；消费蓝筹股已处缓慢筑底回升阶段，但短期动能未必很强。 从当前到明年初，保持向上看的积极态度，同时跟踪四个变量。 美伊局势与油价、美联储利率决策、云厂商资本开支决策、国内内需政策，将影响反弹行情的空间。 一、预期从拥挤转向悲观 主持人：从6月到现在，全球市场发生了哪些重要变化？您怎么看当下的市场？ 陈果： 6月大家最追捧的是半导体，或者说“硅基上游”。之后，费城半导体指数、日韩部分存储和半导体公司，以及A股科技硬件板块，都出现了明显回撤。市场大幅降低了配置和预期，一些代表性的大市值公司在非常短的时间内下跌70%左右，很多A股投资者对于AI硬件的态度发生了接近一百八十度的变化，变得极其悲观，这个反应比我们6月时想的要剧烈。 对于AI硬件尤其是海外算力，过去几个月确实发生了一些变化，导致市场对AI资本开支回报及其持续性的担忧上升。一方面，模型厂价格战升级，头部模型厂收入增速放缓，相关公司的上市融资预期也发生了变化。 另一方面，云厂商的自由现金流压力加大：AI资本开支却没有明显下修，但非AI业务增长低于预期。此外，美联储进入加息周期，中期选举后市场又开始担忧数据中心建设受到更多约束。这些因素对AI硬件的预期确实带来更多挑战。 A股的悲观情绪可能更强一些：在6月因为硅基上游股是所谓牛市走势，那么就配之以牛市思维，因为过去几个月相关板块个股跌幅较大所谓走势已经“技术性走熊”，那么就悲观到底。 好的一面是，A股下半年仍有一些行业取得正收益，例如医药、煤炭、食品饮料。这里有配置再平衡的因素，也有行业自身基本面不错的因素，比如医药中的CXO（医药外包）。资金从集中拥挤在硅基上游，逐步转向挖掘其他行业的机会。 二、硬件担忧有合理性 但AI泡沫破灭的判断不充分 主持人：围绕AI的这些担忧，哪些值得重视，哪些可能被放大了？ 陈果： AI是一个研究和判断难度很高的产业。6月时，我们感受到的是预期过高、交易拥挤，但也很难给出相关公司股价合理定价。 过去几个月，模型厂的价格竞争、收入增速放缓，以及云厂商自由现金流承压，确实加大了市场对资本开支放缓的担忧。这种担忧有合理性。 但云厂商是不是真的会下修资本开支呢？这个无法确认。 资本市场看到的是2027年云厂商自由现金流压力更大，但2028年之后的AI回报，市场是否比产业把握得更清楚更准确呢？ 包括AI硬件与应用，虽然短期看，云厂商如果放缓Capex对于FCF是有利，但中期看，AI应用有突破，云厂商要成长，和AI硬件还是正相关的。 我之前就有一个观点，如果资本市场定价乐观，那么需要警惕，如果资本市场定价悲观，那么AI其实是可以边走边看的。 最后，A股过去几个月对于AI硬件是一个无差别的β级别下跌，海外算力和国产算力的不同细分领域的不同公司，当然有正相关性但不应等于完全一致，甚至应该说还是有明显差别的，A股在后一个阶段的定价，有可能会对这些差异体现出分化的走势。 三、科技以人为本 应用先看局部进展 主持人：您一直强调“科技以人为本”。沿着这个思路，AI下一阶段应该关注什么？ 陈果： 美国中期选举的性质也类似是一次再平衡。美国AI资本积极“跑马圈地”，但对社会的正面作用未被美国民众充分感受到。数据中心除了带来基建就业，产生噪音争夺水资源推高电价推高利率，制造出来的AI则可能要和碳基争夺就业，那这种AI发展模式需要需要审视。 AI的外部性，之前更像是“AI-”，后续需要发展成更多的“AI+”， 需要让更多人切身感受到AI实质改善了碳基生活，也就能得到更多支持。 所以无论是在商业角度还是社会角度，都到了时候需要更多关注怎样把算力转化为应用，转化为能够造福“碳基”的产出。 那由于美国AI CAPEX的体量已经非常大，所以从后续增速和成长性来说，AI应用可能更加突出。或者说AI应用股上涨所需的条件，相比AI硬件更容易满足。 AI硬件正在变成AI的老登，更像一个总量逻辑，需要应用商业化的规模要足够大，才能支撑这么庞大的资本开支还能有较高增长。 AI应用则可以比较分散。AI制药、AI短剧、端侧AI或者机器人，某个领域出现新进展，都可能形成一条投资线索 。 当然硬币的另一面是AI应用整体仍在商业化非常初期阶段，需要耐心资本。 四、市场更理性了，审美也更加多元 主持人：除了AI，您还关注哪些方向的机会？ 陈果：预期收益率不是特别高的话， 各大方向都会有一些细分机会。 我觉得不宜过于强调“主线”思维，“主线”在A股容易被演绎成“ALL IN 单一赛道”，也就容易演绎成拥挤与踩踏。 我认为经历了过去几个月，后面市场的“审美”会多元化一些：既可以看短期增速高的行业和公司，也可以关注真正有护城河、有长期价值的公司。 不必用单一的标准看所有投资机会。更没必要不是全市场ALL IN硬科技，就是全市场ALL IN 红利。 如果是从行业维度看，比如医药依然值得挖掘，中国医药行业本身就有较强的产业竞争力，也一直在进步，未来也很可能受益于AI。 6月后机构增持了CXO龙头，但整个医药板块的配置比例，相对历史水平仍不算高，CXO高景气在继续，而创新药和医疗器械等方向的机会挖掘仍有空间。 再比如，周期类。此前高油价推升通胀和加息压力，市场担心明年全球经济明显下行，很多公司股价表现受限，在A股特别明显。如果明年联储加息次数非常有限，全球经济增长平稳，那么很多周期股有表现机会，包括有色，化工等等。 再比如，内需消费，我认为没必要只是基于顺周期景气度思维予以排斥。6月访谈时，我就提出其实中国消费股已经处于底部。自那以后，一些消费相关行业和公司确实也有一定的正收益。 当然我也不觉得短期内消费股的动能会非常强，它更像是在慢慢筑底回升，这里面的机会会不断增加。比如下半年市场认知到 乳制品的景气度在改善；在承压的白酒行业，也有龙头公司能够提价。还有一些公司受益于行业集中度提升，或者通过出海寻找增量，同时未来肯定要看关注一些新型消费赛道。 当然包括困境反转预期也可以，比如消费电子，今年手机行业面临以旧换新政策退坡、存储涨价等压力。随着时间推移，如果手机存储涨价趋缓，甚至价格下行，再加上未来可能得AI手机、AI眼镜等新品带来新的产品周期，就可能带来戴维斯双击。 从总量逻辑看，我相信一个趋势是作为一个十四亿人的经济体，外需与内需对于增长的贡献不会持续像目前这么明显，明年边际上外需和内需会有再平衡。 五、海外政策的影响还要看实际落地 主持人：美国中期选举等海外政策变化，会怎样影响全球市场，并传导到国内？ 陈果： 从过去的经验看，美联储加息周期对整体港股和A股成长股估值的影响确实不小。中期选举对A股的直接影响没有那么明显，但对美股而言，拉长到半年、一年看，历次中期选举后主要指数上涨的概率比较高。 这次的环境还是相对复杂的。 我认为，从风险偏好看，多了民主党制衡特朗普，边际上减少此前一些难以预判的不确定因素，对于全球市场的稳定性是边际利好。 美国民主党对AI数据中心肯定是边际更严，但最终对AI产业和相关公司价值实质影响能有多大，理论上不至于太悲观，但这确实还需要观察。 假如2028年美国数据中心建设确实受到很强约束，那么相关的州也会推进一些产业增量，例如新能源基础设施，这也可能带来新的机会。 另外民主党看起来不太支持伊朗战争，这对全球市场是一个边际改善的因素，但能否真的结束战争乃至复常，还是要取决于特朗普和伊朗，目前看依然存在不确定性。 六、从当前到明年初，先看修复并跟踪四个变量 主持人：从现在到年底，再到明年初，您对市场和投资节奏有哪些看法？ 陈果： 我觉得以沪深300这类宽基指数为例，结合估值和无风险利率比较，股债性价比仍处于历史较高分位。 短期过去几个月的下跌意味者相当多资金降低了仓位。到了年底、明年初，一些机构有新增资金、需要获得收益，权益仍然是重要选择，红利是肯定有增量资金流入，但股息率下降后，其回报未必能完全满足机构的要求。 因此， 从当前到明年初，仍是一个相对有利的时间窗口。 当然有很多问题判断的难度比较大。比如AI产业可以变化很快，股市演绎得也比较急，A股又是一个喜欢提前反应的市场，很多市场A股在定价的事情可能产业界自己心里都没底，或者说可能相当长一时间很难完全证实，也很难完全证伪。 6月，我对硅基上游还是谨慎的。但在 现在这个位置，A股的预期已经很低，我认为首先应该有一个修复行情，最基础的假设就是超跌反弹 。 即使对半导体，我也暂时看不到短期内足以推动它继续下跌的基本面新因素，目前没有看到主要云厂商对资本开支的态度有明显变化，而产业也可能出现新的进展。 所以我不觉得这个位置还要可以回避半导体，AI硬件也可能参与反弹，可能和AI应用、非AI方向轮动表现。 行情的具体幅度，可以看这些方面是出现超预期： 第一，12月美联储加息情况，以及对明年政策的表态。 第二，美伊局势能否走向缓和，油价能否在明显低于当前的位置形成新的平衡。 第三，云厂商是否下修AI资本开支。 第四，中央经济工作会议对明年内需政策是否会加大支持力度。 最后，看得更长一点，AI依然是最重要的，其可能是一个持续多年的超级周期，其中会经历多轮牛熊交替，与过去熟悉的库存周期、产能周期不完全一样。 就如 6月不宜因半导体指数是牛市走势就说要ALL IN产业革命，也不要因为现在一些指数进入技术性熊市就谈泡沫破灭看空到底。 在当前变化剧烈的环境里，这种思维与操作方式容易犯错。 我倾向于先保持开放的心态，高频观察宏观、产业和政策的边际变化，不能基于过去一个阶段的市场走势就作出很强的大周期判断。 articles.title: Anthropic大清洗：Claude最严封号潮来了！11月12日全面生效
articles.summary: 就在刚刚，Anthorpic开启史上最严大清洗。 官方同步端出全新风控政策，明令封杀非支持地区。 这项新规，将于11月12日正式生效。 就在昨天，Anthropic又是发布了了Fable 5.2，又是正式启动IPO路演。 然而对开发者们来说，真正的震撼弹，是这第三次。 11月12日，三条红线 为什么说这次是史上最狠？ 因为Anthropic彻底撕破了脸，精准狙击许多用户的所有常规路径。 新规中明确指出，任何未列出的国家或地区均不受支持，包括以下三种情况—— 第一，用户在物理位置处于不受支持地区时的使用 ，这包含了（即使是）原本受支持实体的用户和人员。 第二，在不受支持地区注册成立或设立总部的实体，及其用户或人员的使用 ，无论这些个人在物理位置上是否处于受支持地区。 第三，被不受支持地区的个人或实体直接或间接拥有多数股权或控制权的实体的使用 ，包含其用户或人员的使用，无论这些个人在物理位置上是否处于受支持地区。 翻译一下—— 第一，看你「人在哪」（肉身封杀）。 只要你物理位置在不支持地区，哪怕你是合规跨国公司的员工，也禁用。 第二，看你「公司在哪」（注册地/总部封杀）。 公司总部在不支持地区，哪怕员工肉身在美国，也禁用。 第三，看你「背后的老板是谁」（资本/实际控制权）。 这条最绝了，只要你的实体被不支持地区的个人或公司「直接或间接拥有多数股权或控制权」，全面禁用！ 也就是说，如果想去硅谷套壳注册个皮包公司调API，只要查到实控人在国内，那就照封不误。 另外，新规还明确禁止利用消费级订阅转发请求，全面封杀转卖和代理服务。 甚至，这次Anthorpic还搞出第三刀——30天数据留存，「秋后算账」。 以前封号，看的是瞬时IP，而现在，是通过风控看「行为规律」。 现在，新系统会留存30天的安全监控数据。 哪怕今天伪装得极好，但如果你接下来的调用时区、语言特征、多账号并发规律不对劲，系统随时会封禁。 为什么要在这个节骨眼上「痛下杀手」？ 马上要上市的Anthropic，为啥在此时痛下杀手？ 真相藏在Anthropic的IPO文件（S-1）里。 文件赫然披露： 过去9个月，Anthropic居然有 5% 到 7% 的收入，来自事后被认定为「违规」的客户。 这意味着庞大的算力被白白消耗了。 为了给华尔街交出一份干净的招股书，并且堵住核心技术外泄的通道，Anthropic从8、9月份就悄悄拔刀了。 而11月12日，只是最后的时刻。 而开发者们面临的局面，是轻则限速、警告，重则直接拔线、永久封号。 现在，必须紧急备份，导出所有prompt和对话。 然后启动plan B，寻找合规的替代方案。 要敲钟上市的Anthropic，是真把封号做成了一份事业。 本文来源： 新智元 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
